newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Economists voice caution on Taiwan's recovery.
newsitem.headline: Economists voice caution on Taiwan's recovery.

text.p: Taiwan recently raised its economic growth forecast for 1997, helped by an expected increase in private investment, but economists warned on Friday that growth might not be as strong as expected. "The current situation is still showing signs of a gradual recovery," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
But Lin said growth in some sectors could remain tepid.
Firm export and industrial output and a solid real estate market recovery were unlikely, he said.
"The M2 money supply growth and banks' loan approvals are still weak and not enough to support a strong recovery," he added.
On Thursday, the government's statistics agency hiked its forecast for 1997 gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 6.28 percent from 6.20 percent, compared with actual 5.71 percent growth in 1996.
GDP in the fourth quarter of 1996 grew 6.62 percent year-on-year, stronger than a forecast of 6.58 percent. The GDP news boosted Taiwan stocks to a six-year high on Friday.

The statistics agency expected the island's private investment to grow 11 percent in 1997, and government investment to rise 5.3 percent, but some economists voiced their doubts about the strength of the forecasts.
"Government forecasts are always a little bit too optimistic," said Capital Securities economist Wang Chia-yuan.
The revised 1997 GDP forecast would depend largely on whether private and government investment could rise as much as the government expected, Wang said.
The government expected an increase in investment from big enterprises, Wang said, but whether that would occur remained to be seen.
"The government has repeatedly said it will accelerate public construction progress to boost the economy, but whether the progress can go as smoothly as expected is still a question," he said.
Capital Securities expected Taiwan's 1997 GDP to grow 5.9 percent, while National Securities forecast 6.2 percent.
Economists generally did not expect the death on Wednesday of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping to have a strong impact on Taiwan's economy.
However, they said that political uncertainty in China could influence the island's economic growth.

China's President Jiang Zemin was widely expected to hold onto his leadership after Deng's death. But economists said Chinese leaders have already been jockeying for position behind the scenes and potential power struggles may lead to a slowdown in China's economy and hurt Taiwan-China trade.

"If communist China does encounter chaos, its economic growth will surely slow down, thus leading to reduced imports and indirectly hurting cross-strait trade," Chang Yao-tsung, the economics ministry's statistics director, told Reuters.

Trade with China has been a driving force in the island's recent economic expansion. Some 30,000 Taiwan-funded businesses have invested an estimated US$20 billion in China since Taipei began allowing indirect contact with the mainland in the mid 1980s.
China and Taiwan have been diplomatic rivals since a civil war split them in 1949.
